Week 5 — Exploratory Economic Analysis

Week 4 prepared the dataset.

Week 5 uses that prepared dataset to answer economic questions with evidence.

The central question is:

What does the evidence suggest?

This week is not mainly about producing charts. It is about learning how economists move from prepared data to interpretation.

1. Connection to Weeks 1-4

Week 5 depends on everything already covered.

Previous Week Skill Used in Week 5
Week 1 Running Python code and interpreting outputs
Week 2 Understanding variables, observations, and datasets
Week 3 Using logic to classify and test economic rules
Week 4 Preparing analysis-ready data and documenting decisions

The key progression is:

Code -> Data -> Rules -> Prepared data -> Evidence

Week 5 begins the evidence stage.

2. Learning Outcomes

By the end of this week, students should be able to:

  • convert prepared data into economic questions
  • generate descriptive statistics for economic indicators
  • interpret mean, median, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum
  • explain why averages can hide important variation
  • identify distributions, outliers, trends, and crisis years
  • create line graphs, bar charts, histograms, and scatter plots
  • examine relationships between variables using graphs and correlation
  • distinguish association from causation
  • write an evidence-based economic interpretation
  • prepare findings that can be communicated in a Week 6 dashboard

3. Two-Hour Lecture Plan

Time Segment Purpose
0-10 minutes Recap from Week 4 Confirm prepared dataset and new variables
10-25 minutes From data to questions Build analytical questions before coding
25-45 minutes Descriptive statistics Interpret levels, spread, and extremes
45-60 minutes Mean vs median Show why averages are not enough
60-75 minutes Distributions Use histograms to identify concentration and outliers
75-90 minutes Trends and comparisons Use line and bar graphs for time patterns
90-105 minutes Relationships Scatter plots and correlation
105-115 minutes Evidence paragraph Claim, evidence, meaning, caution
115-120 minutes Assignment briefing Prepare findings for Week 6 dashboard

5. Why Week 5 Is Not a Repeat of Week 4

Week 4 asked:

Is the data ready?

Week 5 asks:

What does the data say?

The same dataset is used, but the purpose changes.

Week Main Task Output
Week 4 Prepare data Clean dataset and data-quality note
Week 5 Analyze data Evidence, graphs, interpretation
Week 6 Communicate analysis Interactive dashboard and story

6. Start With Analytical Questions

Good analysis begins with a question, not a graph.

Examples:

  • When did macroeconomic instability become most visible?
  • Which variable shows the largest shock?
  • Did high inflation occur together with negative growth?
  • Did exchange rate changes coincide with inflation?
  • Did reserves fall during crisis years?
  • Which year appears most unusual across multiple indicators?

Weak workflow:

Make graphs first, then search for a story.

Strong workflow:

Ask a question, choose evidence, then interpret carefully.

7. Load and Recreate the Prepared Variables

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kanishkawerawella/ECN4199_Website/main/data/sri_lanka_macro.csv"
data = pd.read_csv(url)

data["Exchange_Rate_Change"] = data["Exchange_Rate"].pct_change() * 100
data["Recession"] = data["GDP_Growth"] < 0
data["Low_Reserves"] = data["Reserves"] < 4000

Inflation classification from Week 4:

def classify_inflation(rate):
    if rate < 5:
        return "Low"
    elif rate <= 15:
        return "Moderate"
    else:
        return "High"

data["Inflation_Category"] = data["Inflation"].apply(classify_inflation)

Quick check:

data.head()

8. Descriptive Statistics as Evidence

Descriptive statistics summarize the dataset.

analysis_vars = [
    "Inflation",
    "GDP_Growth",
    "Exchange_Rate_Change",
    "Reserves",
    "Unemployment"
]

data[analysis_vars].describe()

Interpretation questions:

  1. Which variable has the largest variation?
  2. Which variable has the most extreme maximum or minimum?
  3. Which statistic best identifies the crisis period?
  4. Which statistic is least informative by itself?

9. Mean, Median, and Why Averages Are Not Enough

The mean is useful, but it can be distorted by extreme values.

data["Inflation"].mean()
data["Inflation"].median()
data["Inflation"].max()

Interpretation:

If the mean is much higher than the median, one or two extreme years may be pulling the average upward.

Class discussion:

  1. Would the average inflation rate alone describe the period well?
  2. What does the maximum inflation value add?
  3. Why might the median be more representative of a typical year?

10. Volatility and Standard Deviation

Standard deviation measures spread around the mean.

data[analysis_vars].std()

Economic interpretation:

High standard deviation suggests instability or volatility.

But be careful:

Variables with different units should not be compared mechanically.

Inflation, reserves, exchange rate, and unemployment are measured differently. Interpretation requires economic judgment.

11. Ranking Years by Stress

Sorting helps identify important observations.

data.sort_values("Inflation", ascending=False)
data.sort_values("GDP_Growth")
data.sort_values("Reserves")

Ask:

  • Which year has the highest inflation?
  • Which year has the lowest GDP growth?
  • Which year has the lowest reserves?
  • Do the same years appear across multiple stress indicators?

12. Distribution Analysis

A distribution shows how values are spread.

plt.hist(data["Inflation"], bins=6)
plt.title("Distribution of Inflation")
plt.xlabel("Inflation Rate")
plt.ylabel("Number of Years")
plt.show()

Interpretation questions:

  • Are most inflation values low, moderate, or high?
  • Is the distribution symmetric?
  • Are there extreme observations?
  • What does the distribution suggest about stability?

Weak interpretation:

This is a histogram of inflation.

Better interpretation:

Most years show relatively low inflation, but one extreme crisis year makes the distribution highly uneven.

13. Trends Over Time

Line graphs are useful for time-series questions.

plt.plot(data["Year"], data["Inflation"], marker="o")
plt.title("Inflation Over Time")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Inflation Rate")
plt.show()

Look for:

  • direction of change
  • turning points
  • spikes
  • recovery periods
  • crisis years

Interpretation template:

The line graph shows that [variable] was [stable/increasing/decreasing] until [year], after which [change] occurred. This suggests [economic meaning].

14. Comparing Expansion and Recession

Bar charts are useful for comparing discrete periods.

plt.bar(data["Year"], data["GDP_Growth"])
plt.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
plt.title("GDP Growth by Year")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("GDP Growth")
plt.show()

The zero line matters.

Values above zero indicate expansion. Values below zero indicate contraction.

Ask:

  • Which years are recession years?
  • Which recession is most severe?
  • Do recession years coincide with inflation or exchange rate stress?

15. Comparing Categories

Week 4 created Inflation_Category.

Use it to count years by category:

data["Inflation_Category"].value_counts()

Create a bar chart:

data["Inflation_Category"].value_counts().plot(kind="bar")
plt.title("Number of Years by Inflation Category")
plt.xlabel("Inflation Category")
plt.ylabel("Number of Years")
plt.show()

Interpretation:

Categorical summaries help communicate complex numerical data in simpler terms.

16. Relationships Between Variables

Scatter plots help explore relationships.

plt.scatter(data["Inflation"], data["Exchange_Rate_Change"])
plt.title("Inflation and Exchange Rate Change")
plt.xlabel("Inflation")
plt.ylabel("Exchange Rate Change")
plt.show()

Ask:

  • Do the points move upward together?
  • Is one year far away from the others?
  • Is the relationship driven by a crisis observation?

17. Correlation

Correlation measures linear association.

data["Inflation"].corr(data["Exchange_Rate_Change"])

Interpretation guide:

Correlation Meaning
Close to +1 Strong positive association
Close to 0 Weak linear association
Close to -1 Strong negative association

Important:

Correlation does not prove causation.

Good interpretation:

Inflation and exchange rate change appear associated in the data, especially around crisis years, but this descriptive result does not prove that one caused the other.

18. Building an Evidence Table

An evidence table helps connect claims with numbers.

evidence = data[[
    "Year",
    "Inflation",
    "Inflation_Category",
    "GDP_Growth",
    "Recession",
    "Exchange_Rate_Change",
    "Reserves",
    "Low_Reserves"
]]

evidence

Use the table to support claims.

Weak claim:

The economy was unstable.

Stronger claim:

The economy shows severe instability in 2022, when inflation reached 46.4 percent and GDP growth was -7.8 percent.

19. Evidence-Based Interpretation Framework

Use this structure:

Part Question
Claim What pattern did you find?
Evidence Which numbers or graphs support it?
Economic meaning Why does the pattern matter?
Caution What can the analysis not prove?

Example:

The data suggest that 2022 was the strongest macroeconomic stress point in the period. Inflation reached 46.4 percent while GDP growth fell to -7.8 percent, showing pressure on prices and real economic activity at the same time. This combination matters because households and firms face both rising prices and weaker output conditions. However, this analysis is descriptive and does not prove the exact causes of the crisis.

20. Live Practice Activity

Students should complete this during class.

Part A — Questions

Write three analytical questions about the dataset.

Part B — Statistics

Generate descriptive statistics and identify:

  • highest inflation year
  • lowest GDP growth year
  • lowest reserves year

Part C — Graphs

Create:

  • one histogram
  • one line graph
  • one bar chart
  • one scatter plot

Part D — Interpretation

Write one evidence paragraph using:

  • one claim
  • two pieces of numerical evidence
  • one economic meaning
  • one caution

21. Mini Quiz

Question 1

Why is the average not enough to describe inflation during a crisis period?

Correct answer:

Because the average can hide extreme values, turning points, and year-to-year instability.

Question 2

Which graph is best for showing change over time?

Correct answer:

Line graph

Question 3

Does correlation prove causation?

Correct answer:

No. Correlation shows association, not proof of cause and effect.

22. Common Student Mistakes

Mistake Why It Is a Problem
Reporting numbers without interpretation Does not answer the economic question
Creating graphs without titles or labels Makes evidence unclear
Treating correlation as causation Overstates the result
Ignoring outliers Misses crisis or data-quality issues
Using only averages Hides distribution and instability
Making a claim without numerical evidence Weakens the analysis

23. Responsible AI Use in Week 5

Students may use AI to understand syntax or improve wording, but they must verify the economic interpretation.

Good AI prompt:

I calculated descriptive statistics for inflation and GDP growth. Help me write a cautious interpretation that includes evidence and avoids claiming causation.

Weak AI prompt:

Interpret this data for me.

Students must remain responsible for:

  • selecting the evidence
  • checking the numbers
  • interpreting the economic meaning
  • stating limitations clearly

24. Week 5 Output

By the end of the two-hour lecture, students should have:

  • analytical questions
  • descriptive statistics
  • distribution analysis
  • trend graph
  • comparison graph
  • relationship graph
  • correlation result
  • evidence table
  • one evidence-based interpretation paragraph

25. Bridge to Week 6

Week 6 will use Week 5 findings to build an interactive dashboard.

To prepare, students should identify:

  1. the main story from Week 5
  2. the three most useful indicators
  3. the charts that best communicate those indicators
  4. one caution or limitation

The Week 6 dashboard should not start from scratch.

It should communicate the evidence developed in Week 5.
